Fiberglass vs concrete vs vinyl pools for Florida.

Install time, cost over time, upkeep and durability, compared honestly by a Jacksonville builder.

Get my free 3D design →or call (904) 685-2555

Is fiberglass better than concrete or vinyl in Florida?

For most Northeast Florida families, fiberglass is the best balance: it installs in weeks rather than months, needs the least upkeep and rarely carries a big future repair bill. Concrete is better for truly custom shapes, and vinyl usually has the lowest upfront price. iTop Pools in Jacksonville will tell you if your yard needs something else.

Fiberglass, concrete and vinyl liner pools compared
CompareFiberglassConcrete (gunite)Vinyl liner
Typical installed cost$58,000–$85,000$78,000–$110,000$40,000–$65,000
Ownership cost, 10 yearsRoutine care only, in most casesRoutine care, plus higher chemical and cleaning needsRoutine care, plus possibly one liner ($3,000–$7,500)
Ownership cost, 25 yearsRoutine care and equipment replacementOne or more resurfacings, priced by local quoteOften 2–3 liners ($6,000–$22,500 in total)
Typical install time2–6 weeks after permits3–6 monthsSeveral weeks
Maintenance and chemicalsLowestHighestMedium
Surface feelSmooth gelcoatTextured plaster or pebbleSoft vinyl
Algae resistanceHigh (non-porous)Lower (porous)Medium

Published ranges for typical projects, before deck, enclosure and fencing. Vinyl figures are national because Florida figures were scarce. Ranges vary with size, site and features. iTop gives a firm written price after the site visit.

How long does each pool type take to install?

A fiberglass shell is made in a factory and set in one piece, and Barrier Reef puts a typical install at 2–6 weeks once permits clear. That's less exposed to a Florida summer's rain. Concrete is built on site and commonly takes 3–6 months. Vinyl usually takes several weeks.

Which pool type needs the least maintenance and chemicals?

Fiberglass usually needs the least. Its smooth gelcoat is non-porous, which gives algae less to grip. Barrier Reef estimates vinyl pools use about 50% more chemicals than fiberglass. Concrete's porous surface generally needs the most brushing and chemical attention.

Which pool feels best underfoot?

Fiberglass gelcoat is smooth, vinyl is soft, and concrete has a textured plaster or pebble finish. Texture can look beautiful, but it's rougher on feet and swimsuits, especially for children who spend all day in the water.

How do they handle Florida's soil and water table?

All three types can work in Northeast Florida when they're designed for the site, so the installer matters as much as the material. A fiberglass shell must never be drained without professional advice, because high groundwater can push an empty shell upward. See fiberglass pools and high water tables.

How much can you customize each type?

Concrete has no limits on size or shape, so it's the answer for a vanishing edge or an unusual layout. Vinyl offers many shapes. Fiberglass comes from molds, so you choose from set designs, but Barrier Reef's 22 models cover rectangles, freeforms, kidneys, Roman shapes and plunge pools.

Which should you choose?

  • Choose fiberglass if you want to swim soon, keep upkeep low and avoid big future bills.
  • Choose concrete if you need a shape or size no mold offers, and accept a longer build and periodic resurfacing.
  • Choose vinyl if the lowest upfront price matters most, and you plan for liner replacements.

Sources: Barrier Reef Pools USA (install time, chemical use); published industry comparison guides (concrete build time, liner life). Costs vary by project.

Comparison questions

Fiberglass usually has the lowest long-term ownership cost, because it avoids the two largest recurring bills: concrete resurfacing and vinyl liner replacement. Vinyl liners commonly need replacing every 10–15 years at about $3,000–$7,500 each, and Florida's sun can shorten that. Concrete needs periodic resurfacing and generally more chemicals. Actual costs depend on the pool and how it is cared for.

Concrete is the better choice when you want a vanishing edge, an unusual size or a shape no mold offers. Expect a longer build and periodic resurfacing over the pool's life. If your yard truly needs something custom, iTop will tell you so.

Vinyl usually costs less upfront: Barrier Reef puts fiberglass at roughly 15–20% more than vinyl. But vinyl liners wear out and commonly need replacing every 10–15 years at about $3,000–$7,500 each, so the gap narrows over time. Compare both over the years you plan to own the pool.
